title: Real-Life Haunted Houses? Why People Buy Murder Homes | A&E
excerpt: Some states don't have to disclose what took place at a for-sale property.
content:
Disclose Laws Across America

According to the National Association of Realtors, each state has its own disclosure laws governing what information Realtors are required to disclose about a property’s history, including deaths, murders, suicides or alleged hauntings on the property, and definitions of what constitutes stigmatized property.

“Disclosure laws vary widely state to state,” Liane Jamason, licensed real estate broker and owner of Corcoran Dwellings, in St. Petersburg, Fla., tells A&E Crime + Investigation. “There are some states where you would have to disclose something like murder, and there are others, like Florida, where you really don't have to disclose anything unless it materially affects the value of the property in some kind of way.”

Jamason explains that Florida aims to “protect sellers who say nothing about a death on the property, but that protection only covers the death itself, not any damage it left behind.”

“If a death caused actual physical harm to the house—blood-soaked subflooring, fire damage, structural issues, that's no longer a stigma, that's a defect, and Florida's separate disclosure law requires sellers to reveal known defects that materially affect the property's value,” she continues.

Jamason says that the timeframe for California’s disclosure laws spans just three years, while Alaska and South Dakota just cover the most recent year; some states only require sellers to disclose such information if asked directly.

“Under Illinois law, a stigma like that carries no legal duty to disclose on its own, but if it left a physical trace on the house, the calculus changes, same as Florida,” Jamason says. “Illinois is actually the state where one of the most notorious cases in the country happened, a father who murdered his six children in their Rockford home back in 1978.”

Simon Peter Nelson and the Rockford Murders

In January 1978, Simon Peter Nelson murdered his six children, ages 3 to 12, and the family dog in their home in the historic Churchill’s Grove neighborhood in the center of Rockford, Ill. The murders shocked the community and the nation. Nelson pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity to six counts of murder, but the jury rejected his argument and convicted him of six counts of murder. Although he could have received the death penalty, he was sentenced to six concurrent 100- to 200-year prison terms. Nelson was denied parole 19 times and remained a prisoner until his death in 2017 at age 85.

Since then, the house has sold a handful of times, sometimes occupied by renters, other times, by owners. The Nelson house went back on the market May 1, 2025, and Nate Jordan, chief investment officer of JPM Rockford, jumped at the chance to buy it.

“I happen to own a handful of houses in the neighborhood and on this exact street; I love this area,” Jordan tells A&E Crime + Investigation. “The day it came online, I put an offer in. The realtor did disclose that this house has some history to it, and that was totally fine with us. We understood that history. From our perspective, it was everything we needed it to be.”

Jordan wasn’t the only one who wanted to buy the four-bedroom, two-and-a-half-bath, 2,168-sq-ft. Dutch Colonial house that was built in 1910. It listed for $95,000, a bargain for the sought-after neighborhood, and the seller received multiple offers over asking price.

“We expected there to be at least one other offer, but to have three or four counteroffers definitely shocked me,” says Jordan, who closed the deal in about a week for $115,000. After several months updating and renovating while retaining historic details like built-ins and some of the original bay windows, it was ready for occupants.

Risks and Rewards

Buying a notorious property can be risky.

“Depending on what happened in a home, especially if it’s gruesome, buyers need to consider that it could affect future resale for many years to come,” Jamason advises. “But if it’s a very popular neighborhood in a location with low inventory, maybe [the history] isn’t going to affect it. But if it's in a town with lots of inventory and there's still a strong stigma about it, that could certainly affect the value for many years.”

He also believes that because the murders occurred nearly half a century ago, the notoriety isn’t as worrisome as if they’d happened in recent memory.

“It happened in the ‘70s, when most people in our rental base might not even been 5 or 10 years old, or even alive,” Jordan says. “But we disclosed the history, even if it wasn't top of mind to [potential] renters. The renter that we have in there now is a wonderful woman. She already knew about the house, and that actually attracted her to rent that house. She liked the fact that it had such a history in that it was renovated well.”
